opus_only: For each curve aspect there is a whole-curve version and a version that trades individual local segments of the curve.
Benchmark 2 is a risk-adjusted long S&P position financed by shorting one-month T-bills.
Footnote 3: the weaker expectations hypothesis only requires the expected return gap between short and long strategies to be constant, not zero.
Observed maturities and observation dates are only approximate (e.g. 0.9 or 11.8 months; 28-33 days apart), so the data must be regularised.
Fixed income strategy studies rarely compare with equity investing because of risk, holding-period and credit comparability problems; the equity benchmark here is built to fix that.
Outperformance is tested with paired t-tests and Diebold-Mariano tests on monthly payoff differences.
The benchmarks are charged no transaction costs, a conservative choice for the strategy comparison.
Structuring the trades as notional derivative positions that mirror the cash flows would cut costs substantially.
Level mean-reversion (1-A, 1-B) earns only about 0.27-0.51x the bond benchmark at equal risk, and adding hypothetical maturities makes it worse.
sonnet_only: After costs, only some strategies (2-B clearly) stay significantly better than the benchmarks.
The paper separates directional trades (bets on rate direction) from relative-value trades, and studies only the latter.
Breakeven cost assumes full monthly entry and exit, i.e. maximum turnover.
Yield-curve trading literature is old (from the late 1960s) and broad; authors cite De Leonardis, Freund, Darst, Weberman, Dyl-Joehnk, Stigum-Fabozzi.
Bounded yield curve behaviour is read as evidence of a mean-reverting mechanism; none is identified.
Sample spans 30 June 1964 to 29 December 2000 with 439 monthly curves.
Yields are continuously compounded, at about 1..12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 months maturity.
The unconditional curve is upward sloping and concave, rises over time as new high-rate data enter (Dec-1972 ~4.6% at 1m to 5.6% at 60m; Dec-1986 peak ~6.8% to 7.9%; Dec-2000 ~6.2% to 7.4%).
Start date is dictated by availability of the Lehman Intermediate Government index (Jan 1973).
Duration weighting equalises each maturity's contribution to a parallel shift payoff.
2-A is immune to parallel shifts by construction.
2-B legs are duration-weighted (cash k/(Z-1) per leg) so equal spread changes across pairs give equal payoff.
3-B sizing: k/(X-1) and k/(Z-1) in the wings, 2k/(Y-1) in the belly; funding = k/(X-1)+k/(Z-1)-2k/(Y-1).
Benchmarks are volatility-matched to each strategy before comparing mean payoffs.
Authors claim all trading decisions use only data up to the prior month (expanding unconditional average), so the test is out-of-sample.
Paired t-test needs serially independent payoff differences; positive autocorrelation overstates significance.
Diebold-Mariano statistic tests mean of an autocorrelated difference series; less powerful but weaker assumptions.
Dollar cost (Eq. 4) = 0.00005 x maturity in years x bond value, i.e. 0.5 bp of yield times duration approximated by maturity.
Payoff breakdown by trade segment is shown for 2-B and 3-B.
The 10-11 month spread and 10-11-23 month curvature trades contribute the most profit.
Sub-period view uses a 10-year moving average of monthly payoffs against both benchmarks.
The edge over benchmarks narrowed over time for both 2-B and 3-B.
Conclusion: strategies add significant value to S&P buy-and-hold.
